entry.title: Same Logic, Different Words: Why AI Systems Contradict Themselves, and What We Did About It

link.title: Same Logic, Different Words: Why AI Systems Contradict Themselves, and What We Did About It

entry.content:
Ask a large language model the same question two ways and you may get two different answers. In a paper accepted at NeurIPS 2026, my coauthors and I measured how often this happens, asked why, and tested a fix.

A simple test that strong models fail

Here is a small reasoning problem of the kind we gave the models, dressed in business clothing. A retailer’s shipping policy has two rules, and we know two facts about a customer named Avery.

The facts:

  • Avery does not hold a premium account.
  • Avery made a purchase this year.

The rules:

  • Rule 1. If a customer holds a premium account or is an active customer, that customer qualifies for free shipping.
  • Rule 2. Any customer who has referred a friend or made a purchase this year counts as an active customer.

Does Avery qualify for free shipping? Yes. Avery made a purchase this year, so by Rule 2 Avery is an active customer. An active customer satisfies the “or” in Rule 1, so Avery gets free shipping. The missing premium account does not matter. It is there as a distraction, and a careful reader ignores it.

Written in the notation of logic, with $P$ for “holds a premium account,” $A$ for “is an active customer,” $F$ for “qualifies for free shipping,” $R$ for “referred a friend,” and $B$ for “bought something this year,” the two rules are:

\[ ext{Rule 1: } (P \lor A) ightarrow F \qquad\qquad ext{Rule 2: } (R \lor B) ightarrow A\]

Here the symbol “or” is written as a small v, “and” as an upside-down v, “not” as a hook, and “if … then” as an arrow. The facts are “not $P$” and “$B$.” The chain of reasoning is three short steps: $B$ holds, so $A$ holds by Rule 2; $A$ holds, so “$P$ or $A$” holds; “$P$ or $A$” holds, so $F$ holds by Rule 1.

Now here is Rule 1 again, saying exactly the same thing in different words:

If Avery does not both lack a premium account and fail to be an active customer, then Avery qualifies for free shipping.

That sentence is hard to read, but it is not a different rule. “Not both lacking X and lacking Y” is just a roundabout way of saying “having X or Y.” Logicians call this De Morgan’s law, and it is one of a handful of rewriting rules that every introductory logic course teaches:

\[ eg( eg P \land eg A) \;\equiv\; P \lor A\]

So the rewritten Rule 1 is

\[ eg( eg P \land eg A) ightarrow F\]

which has precisely the same meaning as the original. Any customer who qualifies under one phrasing qualifies under the other. A system that understands the rule, rather than the wording, should give the same answer about Avery either way.

The paper uses three such rewriting rules, applied one at a time and in combination. The other two are even simpler. One replaces “if X then Y” with “not X, or Y.” The other inserts a double negative, turning “X” into “not not X.” Each produces a sentence that sounds different and means the same.

Rule 1 of the Avery example. The diagram asks about the premium account first, then active status.

The picture above is the point of the paper in one glance. However Rule 1 is worded, the questions it asks about a customer, and the order it asks them in, are the same. The diagram is the rule. The sentences are just three ways of describing it.

The Avery problem is adapted from one in the paper, with the subject changed from film history to a shopping account and the logic left untouched. We built a dataset of 1,500 problems with this kind of structure, rewrote each one in several logically equivalent ways using those three rules, and asked some of the most capable models available, including OpenAI’s o3 and Google’s Gemini, to solve both the originals and the rewrites.

They changed their answers often. On the hardest set of rewrites, o3 gave a different verdict on 37 percent of problems compared to the original wording. Gemini flipped on 35 percent. Some of that variation is ordinary randomness in how models generate text, so we measured that too, by asking the same question twice. Randomness accounted for only a few percentage points. The rest came from the rewording.

Figure 3b of the paper. Three models; inconsistency rate on the mixed rewrites versus run-to-run randomness.

The grey bars are the models disagreeing with themselves when asked the identical question twice. The blue bars are what happens when the logic is reworded. The gap between them is the effect of wording.

Accuracy fell as well, by up to 20 percentage points on the rewritten problems. The models were not just inconsistent. They were worse.

Why this matters outside the lab

Most public discussion of AI reasoning focuses on benchmark scores: how many math problems a model solves, how it does on a bar exam. Those numbers matter, but they answer a different question from the one a business faces when it puts a model to work.

In practice, organizations increasingly ask language models to apply rules. Does this claim meet the policy? Has this contract clause been triggered? Should this transaction be flagged for review? Is this applicant eligible? The rule is fixed. What varies is how it is written down, who wrote it, and how the facts of each case are described.

Consider a procurement team that uses a model to decide which vendors need an audit. Again two rules and a few facts, this time about a supplier called Bennett Supply.

The facts:

  • Bennett Supply is a certified vendor.
  • Bennett Supply has no overdue invoices.
  • Bennett Supply missed a delivery deadline last quarter.

The rules:

  • Rule 1. If a vendor is certified and has been flagged for review, the vendor must undergo an audit.
  • Rule 2. Any vendor with overdue invoices or a missed delivery deadline is flagged for review.

The model is asked whether the following statement is true: “Bennett Supply is not required to undergo an audit.” The correct answer is false. The missed deadline triggers Rule 2, so Bennett is flagged. Bennett is certified and flagged, so Rule 1 applies and an audit is required. The clean invoice record is the distraction this time.

With $C$ for “certified,” $G$ for “flagged,” $U$ for “must undergo an audit,” $O$ for “has overdue invoices,” and $M$ for “missed a deadline”:

\[ ext{Rule 1: } (C \land G) ightarrow U \qquad\qquad ext{Rule 2: } (O \lor M) ightarrow G\]

The facts are $C$, “not $O$,” and $M$. The statement to judge is “not $U$,” and it is false because $U$ follows. This problem too is adapted from one in the paper, which uses the same two-rule shape: an “and” in the first rule, an “or” in the second, and one irrelevant fact.

Now suppose the compliance department rewrites Rule 2 as “a vendor is flagged for review unless it has neither overdue invoices nor a missed deadline,” or Rule 1 as “a vendor escapes audit only if it is not certified or has not been flagged.” Nothing about Bennett’s situation has changed. In our experiments, the models’ answers often did.

A system that gives one answer when a policy is written as a list of conditions and a different answer when the same policy is written as a list of exclusions is not reliable, no matter how well it scores on a benchmark. The customer who is denied a refund because the rule was phrased one way, when a colleague with identical facts was approved under the other phrasing, does not care about benchmark scores.

This is a question about trust, and it is a different question from accuracy. A model can be right most of the time and still be untrustworthy if its answers depend on wording rather than substance.

Why models trip

The simplest explanation is that models learn to read wording rather than logic. They are trained on enormous amounts of text, and in text, certain phrasings tend to go with certain conclusions. A model can get very good at exploiting those patterns without ever representing the underlying rule as a rule.

We checked a few alternative explanations. Perhaps the rewritten problems were simply harder? If so, we would expect the models to go from right to wrong far more often than from wrong to right. Instead the flips went in both directions at nearly equal rates. The rewording was not making problems harder. It was scrambling the model’s reading of them.

We also tried the obvious fix: tell the model about the rules of logic. We put the replacement rules, with explanations and examples, directly in the prompt. This did almost nothing. One model improved by under three percentage points. Another got slightly worse. Knowing that two forms are equivalent, in the sense of having been told so, is not the same as treating them as equivalent.

Giving the model a map

If the problem is that models read words instead of logic, one answer is to hand them the logic directly, in a form that does not depend on wording.

Computer scientists have a tool for exactly this. Any rule built from “and,” “or,” and “not” can be drawn as a compact flowchart called a decision diagram. You start at the top, check one fact at a time, follow the branch for yes or no, and arrive at the answer at the bottom. The useful property is that two rules which mean the same thing produce the same diagram, however differently they are written. The refund rule and its rewording above would draw identically.

Our method converts each reasoning problem into its decision diagram, then trains a small companion network to turn that diagram into a numerical summary the language model can consult. We train the companion so that problems with the same logical structure land close together in its summary, regardless of surface wording. The language model then reads this summary alongside the text while it reasons, through a small added component that lets it pay attention to the logical structure when that helps and ignore it when it does not.

Method sketch, simplified from Figure 4 of the paper.

The top row is an ordinary language model. The bottom row is what we add: the same question, turned into its decision diagram, summarized by a small network, and handed to the model as a second input.

The analogy I find useful is a translator who, when given a contract in two languages, is also handed a diagram of what the contract actually commits each party to. The words differ. The diagram is the same. A good translator uses both.

One detail matters for anyone thinking about deployment. Showing the model the diagram as plain text, written out in the prompt, did not work. The gains came only from training the model to use the structure, not from describing the structure to it.

What we found

We tested the approach on two open models, Llama 3.1 and Qwen 2.5, under three different training recipes, so that the result would not depend on one particular setup.

Self-contradiction roughly halved. Under two of the three training recipes, the rate at which a model changed its answer on a logically equivalent rewrite fell from above 30 percent to about 15 percent. Under the third, it fell by several points. The improvement held for every kind of rewriting we tried, not just one.

Table 2 of the paper. Llama 3.1 8B, mixed rewrites; lower is better.

The effect is largest under the two reinforcement recipes, which are the ones most often used to train models for reasoning today.

Accuracy went up, and it went up most on logical forms the model had never seen in training. This is the result I care most about. The model was trained on one family of rule phrasings and evaluated on others. It did better on the new ones because it had learned something about structure, not because it had memorized more examples.

The gains carried over to real-world reasoning benchmarks written by human experts, not just to our constructed data. The companion network trained on our synthetic problems helped on those benchmarks without any retraining.

The approach is also cheap. The companion network is small, and the added component inside the language model adds negligible latency. This is not a bigger model. It is the same model with a better sense of what the question is asking.

One result for the technically curious. When we looked inside the companion network’s summaries, we found that adding a reasoning step corresponded to moving in a consistent direction in the summary space, across different problems. The network had learned to represent “one more step of logic” as a reusable operation, which helps explain why it generalizes.

What this means for anyone deploying AI

Three things, I think.

Consistency is measurable. Before adopting a model to apply a rule, you can test it the way we did: write the rule several equivalent ways and see whether the answers agree. Most teams test accuracy. Few test this, and the two can come apart.

Prompting has limits. Telling a model to reason carefully, or spelling out the logical rules in the prompt, did not fix the problem in our experiments. Some failures are in how the model was trained, and have to be addressed there.

Structure helps. Giving a model an explicit, wording-independent representation of the logic it is supposed to follow made it more consistent and better at generalizing. For high-stakes rule application, that is worth the engineering effort.

This is one paper, on one kind of reasoning, with open models of moderate size. I would not claim more than that. But it points toward a standard for deployed AI that is easy to state: one rule, one answer, however the rule is phrased.

About the paper

“When Form Changes but Logic Doesn’t: Building Logic-invariant LLMs through Structures,” by Xuyuan Liu (Dartmouth), Xinshuai Dong (Carnegie Mellon), Elynn Chen (NYU Stern), and Yujun Yan (Dartmouth). NeurIPS 2026, the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

  • Paper: arXiv:2610.25402
  • Code: GitHub
  • Conference page: NeurIPS 2026

This work was supported in part by the National Science Foundation under grant DMS-2412577.

entry.title: Optimize Once, Execute Fast: Why AI Teams Make You Wait, and How to Fix the Org Chart

link.title: Optimize Once, Execute Fast: Why AI Teams Make You Wait, and How to Fix the Org Chart

entry.content:
The forty-second problem

Picture a customer-support desk that fields ten thousand similar questions a day. The company’s AI answers each one correctly. It also takes forty seconds to do it. Those forty seconds are paid ten thousand times over, every day, and nobody designed it that way. The system was tuned to get the answer right. The delay came along for free.

This is now a common situation. The most capable AI systems in deployment are no longer single models. They are teams. One model reads a request and plans an approach, another drafts the answer, a third checks it for errors, a fourth makes sure it follows company policy. Each member is a specialist, and the division of labor raises the quality of the result. But the request passes through a sequence of hands, and each hand takes time.

For a one-off task, a slow answer is a minor annoyance. For the recurring workloads where businesses actually deploy AI, such as support desks, IT troubleshooting, and code review, the same kind of request arrives over and over, and the delay compounds. A workflow that is a few seconds too slow becomes hours of customer waiting by the end of the week.

Our paper, accepted at NeurIPS 2026, asks a simple question about these AI teams: how much of the waiting is necessary, and how much is just a bad org chart?

Why AI teams are slower than they need to be

Each time a workflow calls a model, it waits for that model to think, and on a busy day it also waits in line behind other requests. In a workflow designed as a chain, every step waits for the step before it. The total time is set by the longest sequence of steps that truly depend on one another. Project managers call this the critical path.

The trouble is that many workflows are longer than their critical path needs to be. A step that checks formatting does not need to wait for a step that checks arithmetic, yet the workflow makes it wait. A second review adds little that the first did not, yet it sits in the sequence. Think of a restaurant kitchen where the cook plating one dish waits for a colleague chopping vegetables for a different dish. Nothing about the food requires the wait. The layout of the kitchen does.

A toy five-step workflow before and after reorganization. The two checks never needed each other's output, and the second style check never needed to exist. Six seconds and three model calls disappear; the answer does not change.

Researchers have built tools that design these AI workflows automatically, but nearly all of them optimize for one thing: getting the answer right. Some also try to reduce computing cost. Very few look at the clock.

What we did

We treat a workflow as a map of who waits for whom, and then edit the map. There are two kinds of edit.

The only two moves the optimizer is allowed to make. Both come with a proof that they can shorten the critical path but never lengthen it.

The first edit lets two steps run side by side when one does not actually need the other’s output. The second removes a step that adds time but not value. Each edit comes with a mathematical guarantee: it can only shorten the longest chain of dependent steps, never lengthen it, and no step loses an input it previously had. We also show that these two edits are enough, in principle, to reach any sensible workflow design from a simple starting point.

Speed alone is not the goal. To keep quality from slipping, we train a small judge that predicts how well a candidate workflow will perform on the task, and we block any edit the judge expects to hurt accuracy. Because the search runs on the map itself rather than by calling the models, finding an improved design takes one to two seconds.

The method works in two modes. It can design a workflow from scratch. Or it can take a workflow a company has already built, including one produced by another automated tool, and make it faster without changing how it was built. That second mode is the one most relevant to firms with AI systems already in production.

What the numbers show

We tested the approach on seven standard benchmarks spanning code generation, math word problems, and general-knowledge questions, against nine alternative ways of organizing an AI team. The reorganized workflows were the fastest on six of the seven benchmarks and had the best accuracy ranking overall. Speed did not come at the expense of correctness.

Seconds per query across seven benchmarks. The orange line is the naive chain where every step waits; gray lines are the strongest prior automated designs; blue is ours.

The starkest comparison came when we swapped in one of the most capable current AI models as the team’s engine. On coding tasks, the reorganized team answered in about 14 seconds. Two widely used alternatives took 40 and 44 seconds and were slightly less accurate. On general-knowledge questions, the gap was similar: about 20 seconds against 33 and 53.

With a frontier model powering every agent, the reorganized workflow is both the fastest and the most accurate on all three tasks.

Used as a bolt-on, the method trimmed three to eight seconds per query from workflows designed by four other approaches, with no loss in accuracy on average. Because redundant steps are removed, the reorganized workflows also consumed less model computation per query, so they were cheaper to run as well as faster.

Applied to workflows that other methods designed, the two edits still shave seconds off, and accuracy nudges up rather than down.

Why “optimize once”

The restructuring has a one-time cost: training the judge and running the search. For the slowest starting designs that cost is recovered after a handful of queries, and every query after that is pure savings. For a workload that repeats thousands of times a day, the arithmetic is not close.

Cumulative waiting time with and without the one-time optimization, using the coding benchmark's numbers. The setup pays for itself before the fourth query.

Why it matters beyond the paper

As companies move from AI pilots to AI in daily operations, response time stops being a technical footnote and becomes a product variable. It shapes whether customers stay on the line, whether engineers trust an automated troubleshooter, and what the computing bill looks like at the end of the month. The design of an AI workflow, which steps run, in what order, and which wait for which, is as much a management decision as an engineering one.

Accuracy and speed are usually presented as a trade-off, where faster means sloppier. Our results suggest that much of the delay in deployed AI teams is organizational slack rather than necessary work, and that it can be removed by reorganizing rather than by cutting corners. The same logic that lets an operations manager shorten a production line applies to a line of AI models.

The work has limits we are open about. It assumes a fixed roster of AI specialists and a stable mix of tasks. Workloads that shift over time, or teams whose members change, will need the method to adapt rather than be rebuilt, and that is where we are heading next.

About the paper

“Optimize Once, Execute Fast: Latency-Aware Multi-Agent Workflow Learning for Recurrent Queries,” by Enpei Zhang (Dartmouth), Feiyu Qu (Dartmouth), Zheng Huang (Dartmouth), Dawei Zhou (Virginia Tech), Elynn Chen (NYU Stern), and Yujun Yan (Dartmouth). NeurIPS 2026, the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

  • Paper: arXiv:2610.14481
  • Code: GitHub
  • Conference page: NeurIPS 2026

This work was supported in part by the National Science Foundation under grant DMS-2412577.
entry.summary: AI systems built from several cooperating models give better answers but take longer to deliver them. In a NeurIPS 2026 paper we show that much of that delay is organizational slack, and that reorganizing the workflow cuts response time by more than half without hurting accuracy.

entry.title: When Generative AI Is Guessing: Separating What a Model Knows from What It Makes Up

link.title: When Generative AI Is Guessing: Separating What a Model Knows from What It Makes Up

entry.content:
Generative AI can produce a thousand plausible-looking forecasts, scenarios, or synthetic records. The hard question is which ones to trust. In a paper accepted at AISTATS 2026, my coauthors and I give a precise answer to a narrower question that turns out to be the right one: for each output, how much of its variation comes from the model not knowing?

Generative models in the back office

Most public attention to generative AI goes to chatbots and image generators. The quieter growth is in generative models that produce numbers rather than words: synthetic demand curves for products that have not launched, simulated price paths for stress-testing a portfolio, artificial sensor traces for equipment that has not yet failed, privacy-preserving stand-ins for customer records that cannot leave a secure environment.

The workhorse for much of this is the diffusion model, the same family of methods behind the leading image generators. A diffusion model learns to produce new samples that look like its training data by starting from pure noise and removing the noise step by step, hundreds of times, until a plausible sample remains. Each run starts from different noise, so each run gives a different sample. That is the point. A planner wants a thousand different demand scenarios, not one.

But the randomness that makes these models useful also hides a problem. When one of the thousand scenarios looks strange, there are two possible explanations. The model may be exploring a real possibility that is simply unusual. Or the model may have wandered into territory it never learned, where it is producing confident-looking output with no basis. A planner needs to know which, and the model’s output alone does not say.

Two kinds of uncertainty

Statisticians have names for these two explanations.

Aleatoric uncertainty is the randomness built into the process. The word comes from the Latin for dice. If you flip a fair coin, there is no amount of additional study that will tell you how the next flip lands. In a diffusion model, the noise injected at each step is aleatoric: it is there by design, and more training data will not remove it.

Epistemic uncertainty is uncertainty about what the model has learned. The word comes from the Greek for knowledge. It arises because the model’s parameters were fit to finite data, and many different parameter settings would have fit that data about equally well. Where those settings agree, the model knows. Where they disagree, the model is guessing. Unlike aleatoric uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty shrinks with more data or a better model.

For anyone deciding whether to act on a generated output, the distinction is the whole game. Aleatoric variation is a feature. Epistemic variation is a warning.

The two can be separated formally. For one step of generation, the total variability of the next state decomposes by the law of total covariance into an average of the within-model randomness plus the variability of the model’s prediction across plausible parameter values. Writing the parameters as theta:

\[\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t-1} \mid x_t) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\big[\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, \theta)\big]}_{\text{aleatoric}} \;+\; \underbrace{\operatorname{Cov}_{\theta}\big[\mathbb{E}(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, \theta)\big]}_{\text{epistemic}}\]

The first term is what a fixed model would do on its own: injected noise. The second is how much the prediction moves when you perturb the parameters within the range the data cannot rule out. Our paper is about computing the second term, and only the second term, for a diffusion model.

That sounds simple. It is not, for two reasons: the second term depends on a distribution over parameters that no one can compute exactly for a modern neural network, and whatever we compute for one step has to be carried through hundreds of steps.

Why diffusion models make this hard

A diffusion model does not produce its output in one shot. It produces a trajectory. Starting from noise at step T, the network predicts how to denoise a little, the sampler applies that prediction plus a fresh dose of random noise, and the process repeats until step 0 yields the sample. A typical run has several hundred steps.

This matters for uncertainty because small modeling errors compound. If the network is slightly unsure at step 400, the state it hands to step 399 is slightly off, and step 399 was never trained on states that are slightly off in that way, so it is slightly more unsure, and so on. By step 0 the accumulated epistemic uncertainty can be large even if no single step was badly wrong. The regions where this happens are predictable in principle: between clusters of training data, at the edges of the training distribution, and anywhere the training set was thin.

The common practical shortcut is to measure total variance across samples and treat it as a proxy for reliability. But total variance is the whole left-hand side of the equation above, aleatoric and epistemic together. A sample can have high total variance because the process is supposed to be random there, and low total variance in a region the model never learned. The proxy does not distinguish the two cases, and in our experiments it misses exactly the samples one would most want to catch.

Isolating the epistemic part

Our method has three ingredients, each with a standard name.

The Laplace approximation. The ideal object is the posterior distribution over parameters: given the training data, which parameter settings are plausible and how plausible is each. For a neural network this distribution is intractable. The Laplace approximation replaces it with a Gaussian centered at the trained parameters, with a covariance that reflects how sharply the training loss curves around that point. Directions in which the loss rises steeply are directions the data has pinned down; directions in which it is flat are directions the data leaves open. Those flat directions are where epistemic uncertainty lives.

Fisher information. The curvature that defines that Gaussian is, for a model trained by squared error, the Fisher information matrix, a quantity that goes back to R. A. Fisher in the 1920s and measures how much the data tells you about each parameter. In a neural network it is approximated by averaging the outer products of the network’s gradients over the training set. Its inverse, lightly regularized, is the parameter covariance we need:

\[\Sigma_{\theta} \;\approx\; (H + \lambda I)^{-1}, \qquad H \;\approx\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} J_i^{\top} J_i\]

Here J_i is the gradient of the network’s output with respect to its parameters on the i-th training example, and lambda is a small constant that keeps the inverse well defined.

Propagation through the trajectory. At each denoising step, we ask how much the network’s prediction would move if the parameters were perturbed within that covariance. The answer is governed by the Jacobian J_t, the sensitivity of the step-t prediction to the parameters. The epistemic covariance of the next state is then the parameter covariance pushed through that sensitivity, and the recursion carries it forward step by step:

\[\Sigma^{\mathrm{ep}}_{t-1} \;=\; a_t^{2}\,\Sigma^{\mathrm{ep}}_{t} \;+\; b_t^{2}\, J_t\, \Sigma_{\theta}\, J_t^{\top}\]

where a_t and b_t are the sampler’s own step coefficients. Throughout, we hold the injected noise fixed, so that the only thing varying is the parameters. This is what makes the quantity epistemic and nothing else. At the end, each generated sample receives a single score, the trace of its accumulated epistemic covariance. A low score means the plausible parameter settings all agree about this sample. A high score means they do not.

The recursion has one simplification: it drops a cross-covariance term between successive steps. We checked this on eighty trajectories and found it changes the score by less than three hundredths of a percent.

Why the usual shortcut fails

The Fisher information matrix for a modern network is enormous: one row and one column per parameter, so a network with ten million parameters has a matrix with a hundred trillion entries. Nobody computes it in full.

The standard workaround is the last-layer Laplace approximation, often abbreviated LLLA. It treats every layer of the network except the final one as fixed and known, and computes the Laplace approximation only over the final layer’s parameters. The final layer is small, so the matrix is tractable. This is the approach taken by BayesDiff, the most widely cited prior method for uncertainty in diffusion models, and by much of the broader literature on Bayesian deep learning.

The trouble is that the final layer is not where most of the uncertainty is. A neural network’s early and middle layers learn the features; the final layer only combines them. If the features themselves are unreliable in some region, because the training data was sparse there, the last layer cannot see that. It reports confidence in a combination of features that were never trustworthy to begin with.

A small example makes this concrete. Train a diffusion model on data that forms nine tight clusters arranged in a three-by-three grid. Then generate samples and score them. Some samples will land between clusters, in regions where there was no training data at all. Those are the samples a good uncertainty score should flag.

BayesDiff assigns low uncertainty to samples between the clusters. The last-layer approximation on its own suppresses the uncertainty even further. Our method assigns high epistemic uncertainty to exactly those between-cluster samples, and filtering by its score leaves samples clustered around the nine modes, as they should be. We also show that for a least-squares problem, the last-layer approximation carries no guarantee of recovering the true epistemic variance, while a random sample of parameters across all layers does.

Figure 1 from the paper. A diffusion model trained on nine tight clusters, then asked to generate new points. Top: uncertainty assigned to each generated sample by BayesDiff (left), last-layer Laplace (middle), and FLARE (right); blue is certain, brown is uncertain. Bottom: the samples that survive filtering at a fixed threshold. Only FLARE flags the points that landed between clusters, where there was no training data.

Figure 1 from the paper. Top: uncertainty assigned to each generated sample by BayesDiff (left), last-layer Laplace (middle), and FLARE (right); blue is certain, brown is uncertain. Bottom: the samples that survive filtering at a fixed threshold.

In the paper’s figure, BayesDiff and the last-layer approximation assign low uncertainty to the samples between clusters, while FLARE assigns them high epistemic uncertainty and removes them on filtering.

A random slice is enough

If computing the full Fisher matrix is impossible and restricting to the last layer is wrong, what is left? Our answer is to pick parameters at random, from every layer of the network, and compute the Laplace approximation over that subset. We call the resulting estimator FLARE, for Fisher-Laplace Randomized Estimator.

The idea is that epistemic uncertainty is spread across the network, not concentrated in any one layer, so a uniformly random sample of parameters sees a representative share of it. Early layers contribute, middle layers contribute, and the final layer contributes in proportion to its actual importance rather than by fiat.

The question a statistician will ask is how large the sample must be. We prove that under standard conditions on the network’s gradient structure, the relative error of the FLARE estimate shrinks at the rate

\[\frac{\big|\operatorname{tr}(\widehat{\Sigma}^{\mathrm{ep}}) - \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{\mathrm{ep}})\big|}{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{\mathrm{ep}})} \;=\; O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\]

where m is the number of parameters sampled. The constants depend on how well conditioned the network’s gradients are and on how evenly information is spread across parameters, in a way the paper makes precise. The practical upshot is that the estimate improves predictably as the budget grows, and in our experiments it stabilizes once ten to thirty percent of parameters are included.

That rate is also what the last-layer approximation lacks. Fixing the subset to the final layer is a particular, non-random choice, and no analogous bound holds for it. The error of the last-layer estimate does not shrink as the layer gets bigger, because the layer was never the problem.

What we found

The practical use of an epistemic score is a filter. Generate many samples, score each, keep the fraction the model is most sure about, and discard the rest. No retraining, no ensembles of models, no repeated sampling.

We tested this on synthetic time series built to probe specific failure modes: sine waves with two competing frequencies, chirps whose frequency drifts over time, and damped oscillations. For each, we trained a diffusion model, generated samples, filtered them with each method, and measured how distinguishable the filtered samples were from real data. The measuring instrument is a separate classifier trained to tell real from generated. If it cannot do better than a coin flip, the generated samples are as good as real.

We report the result as gap closure: the fraction of the classifier’s advantage over chance that filtering removes. One hundred percent means the filtered samples are indistinguishable from real data. Zero means filtering did nothing. Negative means filtering made things worse.

On the sine benchmark, filtering with FLARE closed 93 percent of the gap. The last-layer approximation closed 47 percent. BayesDiff closed 13 percent. On chirps, the figures were 74, 59, and 42 percent. On damped sines, FLARE closed 85 percent, BayesDiff 10 percent, and the last-layer approximation came out at negative 19 percent: it kept the wrong samples.

The filtered samples also look right. On the chirp task, FLARE removes the generated series with spurious oscillations and frequency drift, the kinds of artifacts a domain expert would reject on sight.

The evidence has limits, and the paper says so. The benchmarks are synthetic and low dimensional, chosen to isolate the phenomenon rather than to represent any industry. Extending to multivariate series and images is future work. Curvature estimation remains expensive for the largest models even with subsampling, and the natural next steps are structured sampling and low-rank approximations. None of the experiments use business data.

What this means

For practitioners who generate synthetic data to plan, stress-test, or train other systems, the result is a way to ask a generative model which of its outputs it would stand behind. The score is computed from the trained model as it stands. It requires no second model, no change to the generation process, and no human labeling. In a pipeline that produces thousands of scenarios, it is a cheap first pass that removes the ones the model had no business producing.

For researchers, the contribution is a clean separation that the field had been blurring. Total predictive variance in a diffusion model is not a measure of reliability, because it conflates designed randomness with ignorance. The epistemic term can be isolated, it can be propagated through a long sampling trajectory, and it can be estimated from a random fraction of the network with a convergence rate. The last-layer shortcut, which has become the default in Bayesian deep learning for reasons of cost, is shown to be the wrong default here, both empirically and in theory.

The broader point reaches beyond diffusion models. As generative systems move from producing text we can read to producing numbers we act on, the question of when the system is guessing becomes a question of risk management. It deserves the same precision we would demand of any other forecast.

entry.summary: Generative models are random by design, so their outputs do not reveal when the model is out of its depth. In an AISTATS 2026 paper we isolate the uncertainty that comes from the model not knowing, propagate it through the generation process, and use it to filter out the outputs the model had no basis for.
